lectures.title: Company rule: the Acts from 1773 to 1853

parts.t: The Acts of Company rule at a glance
items: Governor of Bengal → Governor-General of Bengal; Supreme Court at Calcutta provided (established 1774)
Introduced Dual Control (Board of Control for politics + Court of Directors for commerce)
Ended trade monopoly in India (except Tea & China trade); ₹1 lakh annual education grant
Governor-General of India (Bentinck); Law Member added (Macaulay); Company lost commercial role
Last Charter Act; separation of Executive & Legislative functions; Open Competition for Civil Services
**Governor-General of Bengal created:** the Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal (**Warren Hastings**).
**First Supreme Court:** established at Fort William, Calcutta (1774). First Chief Justice: **Sir Elijah Impey**.
**Private trade:** the Act banned private trade / bribes.

parts.t: Pitt's India Act, 1784 and the Act of 1786
items: **Pitt's India Act, 1784 — Dual control:** established Dual Control: Board of Control (political affairs) + Court of Directors (commercial affairs).
**Act of 1786:** Governor-General empowered to override his Council and assume powers of Commander-in-Chief (first enjoyed by **Lord Cornwallis**).
**Trade monopoly:** abolished the Company's trade monopoly in India except for Tea and the China trade (monopoly substantially ended).
**Education:** first time provision made for spending at least ₹1 lakh per year on the education of Indians (₹1 lakh annual grant for Indian education).
**Governor-General of India:** made the Governor-General of Bengal the first Governor-General of India (**Lord William Bentinck**).
**Commercial functions ended:** ended the Company's commercial functions; the Company lost its commercial status entirely.
**Law Member:** added a 4th member as Law Member; first Law Member of the Governor-General's Council: **Macaulay**.
**Section 87:** first opened Company service to Indians without discrimination of religion, colour, etc. (barred discrimination in Company service).
**1813 vs 1833 (Monopoly):** trade monopoly in India was partially abolished in 1813 (retained Tea + China) and completely abolished in 1833.
**Separation of functions:** first time (first clear) separation of the Legislative and Executive functions of the Governor-General's Council.
**Civil Services:** introduced Open Competition for Civil Services.

lectures.title: Crown rule: Acts and council reforms, 1858 to 1947

parts.t: The Acts of Crown rule at a glance
items: Company rule ended; transfer of power to the British Crown; created Viceroy (Canning) & Secretary of State
Indians associated with legislative councils; Portfolio System; Viceroy's Ordinance power; restored Bombay/Madras legislative powers
Budget discussion permitted; limited indirect election principle
Separate Electorate for Muslims; first Indian in Executive Council (S.P. Sinha)
Dyarchy in Provinces; Bicameralism & Direct Elections at Centre
Provincial Autonomy; proposed Central Dyarchy; Federal Court created (established 1 Oct 1937)
Ended British rule; created two independent Dominions (India & Pakistan)
**Company rule ended:** transferred rule from the Company to the British Crown.
**First Viceroy:** the Governor-General was designated as Viceroy; **Lord Canning** became the first Viceroy of India.
**Secretary of State for India:** abolished the Board of Control / Court of Directors; created the Secretary of State for India (assisted by a 15-member Council).
**Law-making:** initiated Indian participation in law-making (Indians associated with legislative councils).
**Decentralization:** restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras.
**Portfolio System and Ordinance:** introduced the Portfolio System and the Viceroy's Ordinance Power (max 6 months).
**High Courts Act, 1861:** High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras established in 1862.
**Budget and questions:** permitted discussion on the Budget and addressing questions to the executive (6 days prior notice); supplementary questions and budget voting were not allowed.
**Separate electorate for Muslims:** introduced by the 1909 Act (Morley-Minto Reforms); **Lord Minto** is called the "Father of Communal Electorate".
**Executive Councils:** first time Indians were associated with the Viceroy's & Governors' Executive Councils.
**Satyendra Prasad Sinha:** first Indian appointed to the Viceroy's Executive Council; the first Indian Law Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council.
**Dyarchy in provinces:** first time introduced dyarchy in the provinces (Provincial Dyarchy: reserved + transferred).
**Dyarchy ("Double Rule"):** system splitting administrative subjects into Reserved (Governor + Executive Council) and Transferred (Governor + Popular Ministers).
**Direct elections and bicameralism:** first time introduced direct elections; first time made the Central Legislature bicameral.
**Responsible government:** first time used the term "responsible government".
**Chamber of Princes:** (120 members) created under the Act of 1919; first Chancellor: **Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner**.
**Provincial autonomy:** introduced Provincial Autonomy and abolished dyarchy in the provinces.
**All-India Federation:** first time provided for an All-India Federation (never came into existence).
**Central Dyarchy:** introduced dyarchy at the Centre (proposed, never implemented).
**Constitutional Autocracy:** introduced by / under the GOI Act 1935 (key detail: constitutional reform).
**Federal Court:** established; inaugurated 1 Oct 1937; first Chief Justice: **Sir Maurice Gwyer**.
**Territories:** separated Burma from India; created Sindh & Orissa as new provinces.
**Ordinance power:** the Act is the basis for the President's Ordinance Power (Art. 123).
**Partition into India & Pakistan:** ended British sovereignty (British rule); created two independent Dominions (India and Pakistan).
**Constituent Assemblies:** given dual constitution-making and legislative powers.
Abolished in Provinces; Proposed at Centre
**1919 vs 1935 (Dyarchy):** Provincial Dyarchy = 1919; Central Dyarchy proposed = 1935.
**1861 vs 1935 (Ordinance):** the Viceroy's Ordinance power originates in the Indian Councils Act, 1861, whereas Art. 123 of the Indian Constitution is modeled after Section 42 of the GoI Act, 1935.

lectures.title: The Constituent Assembly and the making of the Constitution

parts.t: The demand for a Constituent Assembly
items: Officially demanded at Patna (May 1934); Nehru's clear statement in 1938
**Total seats planned:** 389 (296 British India + 93 Princely States).
**British India seats:** 292 from Governor's provinces + 4 from Chief Commissioners' provinces.
**Elections held:** July–August 1946; indirect election (members elected by Provincial Legislative Assemblies).
**Franchise:** not based on Adult Franchise (restricted franchise under GoI Act 1935 – tax, education, property).
**Princely States:** initially stayed away; started joining from the third session (April 1947).
**First Finance Minister of Independent India:** R.K. Shanmukham Chetty (some sources also mention John Mathai later).
B.N. Rau (prepared first draft – 243 Articles, 13 Schedules)
**First draft:** the first draft of the Constitution was prepared by Constitutional Advisor **B.N. Rau**.
First meeting of the Constituent Assembly (temporary President: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha)
Permanent President elected → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
Jawaharlal Nehru moved (introduced) the Objectives Resolution (5th meeting of 1st session)
Objectives Resolution unanimously adopted by the Assembly
Drafting Committee constituted under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
Constitution of India adopted and enacted (Constitution Day); last day of 11th session
Last (final) meeting of the Constituent Assembly (signatures); National Anthem adopted
Constitution fully came into force; Republic of India established
**Total sessions:** 11 (165 sitting days) + final meeting on 24 Jan 1950.
**Constituted:** 29 August 1947. **Chairman:** Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. 7 members total; prepared the draft Constitution.

**Other members (6):** Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, K.M. Munshi, Mohammad Saadullah, B.L. Mitter (later replaced by N. Madhava Rao), D.P. Khaitan (later replaced by T.T. Krishnamachari).

Federal legislative division; federal subject distribution
Committee on negotiations with Princely States

lectures.title: Features of the Constitution: borrowed sources and the Rule of Law

parts.t: Forms of government and the main blueprint
items: **Parliamentary form of government:** first introduced in Great Britain.
**Presidential form:** first formed in the USA.
**Government of India Act, 1935:** the main blueprint; structural & administrative backbone (Federal scheme, Governor, Judiciary, Emergency, PSC, etc.).

parts.t: Features borrowed from Britain and the USA
items: Parliamentary form of Government (Parliamentary system); Rule of Law; Cabinet System; Single Citizenship; Bicameral Legislature (Bicameralism); Parliamentary Privileges; Prerogative Writs
Fundamental Rights; Judicial Review; Independence of Judiciary; Preamble (idea); Post of Vice-President; Impeachment of President; Removal of Judges of SC & HC

**India vs UK constitutional model:** India: Constitutional Supremacy + Judicial Review of primary legislation; United Kingdom: Parliamentary Sovereignty (no striking down of primary parliamentary statutes).
Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP); Method of election of President; Nomination of members to Rajya Sabha
Federation with strong Centre; Residuary powers with Centre; Appointment of Governors by Centre; Advisory jurisdiction of Supreme Court
Concurrent List; Joint sitting of both Houses; Freedom of trade, commerce & intercourse; Language of the Preamble
Procedure for Constitutional Amendment; Election of members of Rajya Sabha
Fundamental Duties; Ideals of Justice (Social, Economic & Political) in Preamble
Republic; Ideals of Liberty, Equality & Fraternity in Preamble

parts.t: Rule of Law: origin and Dicey's three elements
items: **Philosophical origin & jurist:** propounded by British constitutional jurist **A.V. Dicey** in *Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution* (1885).
**Constitutional origin / borrowing:** borrowed from the British Constitutional System (alongside Parliamentary Government, Single Citizenship, Cabinet System, and Prerogative Writs).

**1. Absence of Arbitrary Power (Limitation of Powers):** absolute supremacy/predominance of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary power; no man can be punished except for a distinct breach of law established in ordinary legal manner.
**2. Equality Before the Law (Equal Subjection):** equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land administered by the ordinary law courts; no one is above the law.

**3. Primacy of the Rights of the Individual (Liberty & Civil Rights):** the Constitution is the result of the rights of individuals as defined and enforced by the courts, rather than the source of individual rights.

**Dicey's Third Principle in India:** in the UK, the Constitution is the result of judicial decisions on individual rights; in India, the Constitution is the Source of Rights (reversing Dicey's third premise while adopting the first two intact).

parts.t: Rule of Law: traps and conceptual pairs
items: "State has inherent unlimited police powers" - FALSE
"Executive officials are subject only to special administrative tribunals" - FALSE (Dicey opposed French Droit Administratif)
**Primacy of the Rights of the Individual**
"People's responsibility to the Government" is NOT a pillar of Rule of Law → FALSE
**Trap — option component:** "People's responsibility to the government" → DELETE (Rule of Law restrains the government, not expands citizens' obedience to authority).
**Rule of Law:** Government itself is subordinate to the law; laws must be just, fair, and non-arbitrary (Government under Law).
**Rule by Law:** law is used purely as an instrument/weapon of state control to govern citizens while the ruler remains above it (Government above Law).
**Constitutional Government:** synonymous with Limited Government—power is defined, restrained, and checked by constitutional provisions to prevent executive tyranny.
**Rule of Law vs. Public Interest Litigation (PIL):** PIL promotes and strengthens access to justice for the disadvantaged, but is NOT an indispensable prerequisite for the existence of Rule of Law.
**Before PIL:** Rule of Law existed prior to PIL evolution via Arts. 14, 32, and 226.
